title: Copywriting for Sales
subtitle: Write clear, honest sales copy for WhatsApp, Instagram, ads, web pages and email that turns interested people into paying customers.
description: Learn to find your customer's real pain points, turn features into benefits and use proven frameworks such as AIDA, PAS and Before-After-Bridge. Through many before-and-after examples from Nigerian small businesses, you will write headlines, product descriptions, captions, calls to action, ads, sales pages, broadcasts and emails, then edit and A/B test them to learn what works.
outcomes: Build a customer profile of pain points, desires and objections from real chats and comments
Turn product features into benefits and write headlines that pass the 4 U's check
Write WhatsApp status series, Instagram captions, product descriptions and calls to action that make ordering easy
Plan Facebook and Instagram ads, one-page sales pages, WhatsApp broadcasts and email sequences using AIDA and PAS
Use stories, objection answers and testimonials honestly and within consumer protection and data protection rules
Edit copy with a checklist and run a fair A/B test to choose the better version
audience: Women who sell products or services, or help others sell, mostly through WhatsApp, Instagram and Facebook, and want more replies and orders from what they write.
tools: A smartphone with WhatsApp Business and Instagram or Facebook
A notebook or phone notes app
Google Sheets or a paper table for recording test results
Optional: a free email tool such as Mailchimp, Brevo or MailerLite
Optional: a Paystack, Flutterwave or Selar account for payment links

modules.title: Foundations of Persuasive Writing
modules.overview: Before you write a single caption, you need to know what sales copy is for, who you are writing to and what they are struggling with. This module covers the job of copy, how to find your customer's real pain points, how to choose a voice, and the honest psychology that makes people say yes.

lessons.title: What sales copy does: one reader, one offer, one action
objectives: Explain the difference between sales copy and general content
Identify the reader, the offer and the action in any piece of copy
Rewrite a weak product message so it speaks to one customer
Apply the 'so what?' test to your own sentences

blocks.text: **Copywriting** is writing that asks someone to do something: buy, order, send a message, book, register or visit. The words on a WhatsApp status, a flyer, an Instagram caption, a product label or a Facebook ad are all called **copy**. The person who writes them is a **copywriter**. If you sell anything, you are already a copywriter. This course will help you do it on purpose.

General content informs or entertains. Sales copy has a job. A recipe post teaches how to make zobo. A sales post for your zobo tells a busy office worker in Yaba why your chilled zobo will save her afternoon and how to order before 11am. Both can be good writing, but only one is built to produce an order.

blocks.name: writer
blocks.alt: A woman writing at a desk
blocks.caption: Every seller who writes a status, caption or flyer is doing copywriting, whether she calls it that or not.

blocks.text: The three things every piece of copy needs

items: **One reader.** Picture one real person, not 'everybody'. Copy written for everybody speaks to nobody.
**One offer.** What exactly are you selling, at what price or package, and what makes it worth it?
**One action.** What should she do next? 'Send me a WhatsApp message with your size' is an action. 'Patronise us' is not.

blocks.text: When copy fails, one of these three is usually missing. Look at the common status message 'Quality bags available. DM for price.' Who is it for? What bag? Why this bag? The only action is to ask for a price, which many people will not bother to do.

blocks.title: Worked example: a bag seller's status, before and after
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi sells ladies' work bags from her shop in Onitsha and posts on WhatsApp status every morning. Her old status gets views but almost no messages.
steps: Before: 'Quality bags available. DM for price. We deliver nationwide.'
She chooses one reader: a young woman starting her first office job who needs one bag that fits a laptop and looks smart.
She chooses one offer: a black faux leather tote that fits a 15-inch laptop, priced at about N18,500 (her current price, which she updates when it changes).
She chooses one action: reply with the word TOTE to reserve one.

After: 'Starting a new job? This black tote fits your 15-inch laptop, charger and lunch pack, and still looks neat in meetings. N18,500. Only 6 left in black. Reply TOTE and I will hold one for you till 6pm today.'
blocks.result: The new status names the reader's situation, gives the real price, shows proof of usefulness (what fits inside) and asks for one easy action. People who reply TOTE have told her they are interested, so she can follow up personally.

blocks.text: The 'so what?' test

Read each sentence you write and ask, as your customer would: **so what?** 'Our hair cream contains shea butter.' So what? 'So your edges stay soft between washes.' Now the sentence matters to her. If you cannot answer 'so what?', the sentence is either missing its benefit or it does not belong. You will use this test throughout the course, and in Module 2 we will go deeper into features and benefits.

blocks.title: How copy turns a viewer into a buyer
items: She notices it
She reads on
She believes it
She takes action
blocks.caption: Each line of your copy should move the reader one step along this path, or it is slowing her down.

blocks.text: Copy is selling in writing

Think of how you sell face to face in the market. You greet the customer, notice what she is looking for, show her the item, answer her worries about price or quality, and then ask, 'Shall I wrap it?' Good copy does the same, except the customer cannot ask you questions. So your words must answer her questions before she asks them: what is it, is it for me, does it work, how much, how do I get it, and can I trust you?

head: Customer's silent question
What your copy should answer
rows: Name the product plainly: 'Unripe plantain flour, 1kg pack'
Name her situation: 'For anyone managing their weight who misses swallow'
Does it work or is it good?
Give proof: ingredients, photos, a real customer comment
State the price or the price range clearly
Say how to order, pay and receive it
Show your shop address, reviews, delivery record, return policy

blocks.title: Show the price when you can
blocks.text: Many Nigerian sellers write 'DM for price'. Some buyers will message, but many scroll on, because asking feels like a commitment. If your price is fixed, show it. If it changes with size or quantity, show a starting price, for example 'from N4,000'.
What good copy is not

Good copy is not shouting. Writing everything in capital letters, adding ten emojis or saying 'BEST IN NIGERIA!!!' does not persuade a careful buyer. It is also not lying. A false claim may bring one sale, but it costs you the customer and her friends. The best copy is clear, specific and true, written by someone who understands the buyer's problem.

takeaways: Copywriting is writing that asks a reader to take an action
Every piece of copy needs one reader, one offer and one action
Use the 'so what?' test to turn facts into reasons to buy
Answer the buyer's silent questions before she has to ask

activity.title: Rewrite one real status
steps: Copy the last sales status or caption you posted into your notebook or phone notes.
Write down who the one reader is, what the one offer is and what the one action is. Leave a blank where any is missing.
Apply the 'so what?' test to every sentence and add the benefit where it is missing.
Rewrite the message so it names the reader's situation, the price and one clear action.
Post the new version and note how many replies it gets compared with your usual posts.
activity.evidence: A note or screenshot showing the old message, the new message and the number of replies each received

lessons.title: Finding your customer's pain points and desires
objectives: Define pain points, desires and objections in plain words
Collect your customer's real words from chats, comments and conversations
Build a one-page customer profile for one product
Turn a pain point into an opening line for copy

blocks.text: People do not buy products. They buy a better situation. A mother does not want a blender; she wants to stop grinding pepper on the stone every Saturday. A trader does not want a POS machine; she wants to stop losing customers who have no cash. Your copy works best when it starts with the situation your customer wants to escape or reach.
Three things to know about your customer

items: **Pain points:** the problems, frustrations or worries she has right now. Example: 'My children's school shoes tear before the term ends.'
**Desires:** what she wants instead. Example: 'Shoes that last the whole term and still look neat on visiting day.'
**Objections:** the reasons she might not buy from you. Example: 'Online sellers send different shoes from the picture.'

blocks.name: target-audience
blocks.alt: A person pointing at a group of customer profiles
blocks.caption: Your copy gets sharper when you write for one clear customer instead of a crowd.

blocks.text: Use the customer's own words

The best copy often sounds like something the customer already said. Copywriters call this **voice of customer** research. You do not need a survey company. You already have the material in your phone.

items: Scroll through your WhatsApp chats with customers from the last three months. Copy every question and complaint into one note.
Read the comments under your posts and under competitors' posts on Instagram, Facebook and TikTok. Note the words people use.
Read reviews of similar products on Jumia or Google Maps listings. Note what people praise and what they complain about.
Ask three loyal customers two questions: 'What made you buy the first time?' and 'What almost stopped you?' Write down their exact words.
Group what you collected into pains, desires and objections.

blocks.title: Respect privacy
blocks.text: Use customers' words to understand them, but do not post their names, numbers or chat screenshots without their clear permission. Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023 requires a lawful basis, such as consent, for using people's personal data.

blocks.title: Worked example: from chats to a headline
blocks.context: For example, Aisha makes unripe plantain flour in Kaduna and sells 1kg packs. She reads 40 chats from the last two months.
steps: She finds the same questions again and again: 'Will it taste bitter?', 'Is it okay for my father who is diabetic?', 'Is it really plantain or mixed with something?'
Pain point she sees most: people told by a doctor to change their swallow, who miss eating swallow with soup.
Desire in their words: 'I just want to eat swallow without feeling guilty.'

Objections: bitterness, purity, and whether it is safe for a health condition. She notes that she must not make medical claims; she can only describe the ingredient honestly and suggest buyers follow their doctor's advice.
Before: 'Buy our plantain flour, 100% natural.'
After: 'Miss eating swallow? Our unripe plantain flour is made from only dried unripe plantain, nothing added. Smooth, not bitter, and ready in 5 minutes. Ask your doctor how it fits your meal plan.'
blocks.result: The new copy opens with the reader's own feeling ('miss eating swallow'), answers the purity objection directly and handles the health question honestly instead of making a claim she cannot prove.

blocks.title: Pain point versus desire
items: Pain point (now)
Desire (after)
blocks.caption: Strong copy names where the customer is now and paints where she wants to be.

blocks.text: Build a one-page customer profile
Write a short profile for each main product. Give your imaginary customer a first name so you can picture her. Keep it real and based on what you learnt, not on guesses.

head: Profile item
Example for school shoes
rows: Funmi, mother of three in Ibadan, works at a bank
Cheap shoes tear before term ends; buying twice costs more
One pair that lasts the term and looks neat
Afraid the shoes delivered will not match the photo
WhatsApp status at night, Facebook groups for parents
'Strong', 'last the whole term', 'my son is rough with shoes'

blocks.text: Turn the pain into an opening line

Once you know the pain point, your first line can name it. A question works well when the answer is obviously yes for the right reader: 'Is your son rough with school shoes?' A statement works too: 'If you bought school shoes twice last term, this is for you.' The reader who has that problem stops scrolling because she feels seen. The reader who does not have it scrolls on, and that is fine.

blocks.title: Do not exaggerate the pain
blocks.text: Naming a real problem is helpful. Inventing fear is manipulation. Avoid lines like 'Your child will be laughed at in school' or false health scares. They damage trust and can break advertising rules.

Update your profile every few months. Customers change, prices change, and new worries appear. When fuel prices rose, for example, many buyers started asking about delivery costs first. A seller who notices that early can address delivery in her copy before anyone asks.

takeaways: Customers buy a better situation, not just a product
Know three things: pain points, desires and objections
Your chats, comments and reviews are free customer research
Open your copy with the customer's own words about her problem

activity.title: Make a customer profile from real chats
steps: Pick your best-selling product.
Read at least 20 customer chats or comments about it and copy every question or complaint into a note.
Sort them into pains, desires and objections.
Fill in the six-row customer profile table for that product.
Write three possible opening lines that use the customer's own words.
activity.evidence: Your completed customer profile and the three opening lines, saved as a note or photo of your notebook

lessons.title: Choosing a brand voice and matching tone to the moment
objectives: Explain the difference between voice and tone
Describe your brand voice in three words with do and don't rules
Decide when to use Pidgin, local languages or standard English
Adjust tone for promotions, apologies and serious messages

blocks.text: Imagine two food sellers. One writes: 'Dear esteemed customers, kindly be informed that our jollof rice is now available.' The other writes: 'Jollof wey go make you forget your problems is ready. Party flavour, plenty pepper. Order before 1pm.' Both sell jollof. They sound like two different people. That difference is **voice**.
Voice and tone are not the same

**Voice** is your brand's personality. It stays the same across everything you write, the way your friends recognise you on the phone before you say your name. **Tone** is how that voice adjusts to the situation. You speak differently at a wedding and at a condolence visit, but you are still you.

blocks.name: content-creator
blocks.alt: A woman creating posts on her phone and laptop
blocks.caption: Your voice is what makes your posts recognisable even before customers see your name.

blocks.text: Describe your voice in three words

Choose three words that describe how you want customers to feel about your brand. Then write what each word means in practice, and what it does not mean. This stops your voice drifting from post to post.

head: Voice word
We do
We don't
rows: Greet people, thank them, use 'you' and 'we'
Sound cold, use stiff phrases like 'be informed'
State facts clearly: 'This fabric does not fade'
Use light humour and the occasional Pidgin line
Make jokes about customers or sensitive topics

blocks.title: Worked example: one message, three voices
blocks.context: For example, three different businesses announce that they now deliver to Lekki and Ajah on Saturdays.
steps: A children's clothing brand with a warm, gentle voice: 'Good news for our Lekki and Ajah mums: we now deliver every Saturday. Order by Friday 5pm and your little one's outfit arrives in time for Sunday.'
A streetwear brand with a bold, playful voice: 'Lekki, Ajah, una don dey call us. We hear you. Saturday delivery don land. Order by Friday, wear am Sunday.'
A corporate catering company with a professional voice: 'We now offer Saturday delivery to Lekki and Ajah. Orders confirmed by Friday at 5pm will be delivered between 9am and 1pm on Saturday.'
blocks.result: The facts are identical in all three (areas, day, cut-off time). Only the voice changes, and each one fits its customer. Notice that all three still give the specific details a buyer needs.

blocks.text: Pidgin, local languages or standard English?

Write in the language your customer uses when she is relaxed and buying. Nigerian Pidgin can feel friendly and close for many audiences, especially for food, fashion and entertainment. Yoruba, Hausa, Igbo or other local languages can build strong connection in a local market. Standard English may suit corporate buyers, professional services, health-related products and older customers. Many sellers mix them: a Pidgin hook, then clear English details.

items: Keep prices, dates, sizes and payment details in clear, simple English or numbers so nobody misreads them.
Only write in a language or style you know well. Badly written Pidgin sounds fake.
Test both: post the same offer in two styles on different days and see which gets more replies. Module 4 shows how to test properly.

blocks.title: Choosing tone for the moment
items: Celebrations and new arrivals
Sales and promotions
Apologies and delays
Policy and price changes
blocks.caption: Your voice stays the same, but your tone moves around this map depending on what you need to say.

blocks.text: Tone for difficult messages

Tone matters most when something goes wrong. If a delivery is late, a joke can feel like you do not care. Use a calm, direct and respectful tone: say what happened, say what you are doing about it, and say what the customer can expect.

blocks.title: Worked example: an apology for late delivery
blocks.context: For example, Blessing runs a cake business in Port Harcourt. Heavy rain delayed three birthday cake deliveries by two hours.
steps: Before: 'Sorry o, rain did us. Cake is coming.'
She removes the casual line, because a birthday is important to the customer.

After: 'I am very sorry. The heavy rain on the East-West Road has delayed our driver. Your cake is safe and packed, and he expects to reach you by 4:30pm. I will send you his location now. As an apology, your next order of small chops is free.'
blocks.result: The customer knows the reason, the new time, how to track the cake and what Blessing is offering to make up for it. Her voice is still warm, but the tone is serious.

blocks.text: Words to avoid in almost every tone: 'kindly be informed', 'we regret any inconvenience this may have caused' and other stiff phrases. They sound like a form letter. Say it the way a respectful person would say it face to face: 'I am sorry your order is late. Here is what I am doing about it.'

blocks.title: Write a mini style guide
blocks.text: Put your three voice words, your do and don't table, and your language choices on one page. Share it with anyone who helps you post, so your brand sounds the same even when you are busy.

takeaways: Voice is your brand's steady personality; tone changes with the situation
Describe your voice in three words with clear do and don't rules
Write in the language your customer relaxes and buys in, and keep key details in plain words
Use a calm, direct tone for apologies and serious news

activity.title: Create your one-page voice guide
steps: Write three words that describe how you want customers to feel about your brand.
For each word, write one thing you do and one thing you do not do in your writing.
Decide which language or mix you will use for hooks and which for details.
Rewrite one recent post so it matches your voice guide.
Write a short template for apologising when an order is delayed.
activity.evidence: Your one-page voice guide and the rewritten post, saved as a photo or document

lessons.title: The psychology of persuasion: benefits, AIDA and honest influence
objectives: Turn product features into benefits using the 'which means' bridge
Use the four AIDA steps to plan a short sales message
Recognise six common principles of influence and use them honestly
Avoid manipulative tactics that destroy trust

blocks.text: People decide with feelings and then justify with facts. That does not mean customers are foolish. It means your copy must do two jobs: help her **feel** that the product solves her problem, and give her the **facts** to feel safe saying yes.
Features and benefits

A **feature** is a fact about the product: what it is or has. A **benefit** is what that feature does for the customer. A simple bridge connects them: write the feature, then add '**which means**' and finish the sentence from the customer's point of view.

head: Feature
Which means (benefit)
rows: You can sleep through the night even when NEPA takes light
Adire fabric dyed with fixed colour
It still looks bright after many washes
You do not cook after work from Monday to Friday
Customers who carry no cash can still buy from you

blocks.text: Some features need more than one 'which means' step. 'Stainless steel pot' leads to 'which means it does not rust', which leads to 'which means you buy one pot and use it for years'. Keep going until you reach something the customer truly cares about. Then keep the feature in the copy as proof.

blocks.name: thinking-face
blocks.caption: Customers think 'what is in it for me?' Benefits answer that question.

blocks.text: AIDA: a map for any sales message

**AIDA** is one of the oldest models in advertising. It stands for Attention, Interest, Desire and Action. It describes the steps a reader goes through before buying, and it gives you an order to write in.

items: **Attention:** a first line or image that makes the right person stop. Often it names her problem or a strong benefit.
**Interest:** a few details that make her want to know more. What is it? How is it different?
**Desire:** benefits, proof and a picture of her life with the product.
**Action:** one clear instruction, with any honest reason to act now.

blocks.title: AIDA: from many viewers to a few buyers
items: Attention: many people notice
Interest: some read on
Desire: fewer want it
Action: buyers respond
blocks.caption: Each stage loses some readers, so every line must earn the next one.

blocks.title: Worked example: AIDA for a tailoring service
blocks.context: For example, Halima is a tailor in Kano who sews ready-to-wear kaftans for men and wants more orders before Sallah.
steps: Before: 'We sew kaftans. Contact us.'
Attention: 'Sallah is in 3 weeks. Is your kaftan ready?'
Interest: 'We sew men's kaftans in 5 days from your measurements, using cotton that does not shrink after washing.'
Desire: 'Neat embroidery on the neck and cuffs, sized to fit, so you look sharp at Eid prayers and family visits. See photos of last year's orders in my catalogue.'
Action: 'I can take 15 more orders before Sallah. Send your measurements on WhatsApp today with the word KAFTAN.'
blocks.result: The message follows the reader's thinking from 'this is about me' to 'I want this' to 'I know exactly what to do'. The 15-order limit is honest because Halima can only sew so many in time.

blocks.text: Six principles of influence
Psychologist Robert Cialdini described six principles of influence in his well-known book Influence. Used honestly, they help buyers make decisions. Used dishonestly, they become tricks.

head: Principle
Honest use in copy
Dishonest use to avoid
rows: Share real reviews and photos from real customers
'Only 8 pieces left in this fabric' when true
Saying 'last few' every day for months
Mention your real training, NAFDAC number or years of experience
Claiming certificates you do not have
Give a free useful tip, sample or guide
Ask a small step first: 'Reply YES for the price list'
Pressuring people after a small yes
Show your face, your story and your team
Pretending to be someone you are not

blocks.text: Manipulation to avoid

items: **Fake countdowns:** a 'sale ends tonight' message that you repeat next week with the same offer.
**Shaming:** copy that makes people feel ugly, poor or stupid so they buy. It may work once, but it builds resentment.
**Hidden costs:** showing a low price and adding delivery, packaging or 'service charge' only after payment.
**Pressure after payment questions:** if a buyer asks for time to think, give it. A short follow-up later is fine; ten messages in a day is not.

blocks.text: A simple check before you post: would you be comfortable if the customer later saw exactly how and why you wrote each line? If the answer is yes, your persuasion is honest.

blocks.title: Honesty is also the law
blocks.text: Nigeria's Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC) enforces consumer protection law that forbids false or misleading claims about goods and services. False 'limited time' offers, fake reviews and exaggerated health claims can get you into trouble as well as lose you customers.

takeaways: Features are facts; benefits are what those facts do for the customer
Use 'which means' to turn every feature into a benefit
AIDA gives you an order: Attention, Interest, Desire, Action
Social proof, scarcity and the other principles work only when they are true

activity.title: Write an AIDA message for one product
steps: List five features of one product you sell.
Turn each one into a benefit using 'which means'.
Write a four-line message: one line each for Attention, Interest, Desire and Action.
Add one honest influence principle, such as a real review or a true stock limit.
Read it aloud and remove any word that sounds like exaggeration.
activity.evidence: Your feature and benefit list and your four-line AIDA message

quiz.q: Ngozi's status says 'Quality bags available. DM for price.' Which of the three essentials is MOST clearly missing?
options: A specific reader and offer
A logo
Emojis
A long story
quiz.explain: The status does not say who the bag is for or which bag it is, so no reader feels it is meant for her. A clear reader, offer and action matter far more than a logo or emojis.

quiz.q: Which sentence turns the feature 'contains shea butter' into a benefit?
options: Contains 100% pure shea butter
Shea butter is sourced from the North
Keeps your edges soft between washes
Shea butter is very popular
quiz.explain: A benefit says what the feature does for the customer. Soft edges between washes is the result she cares about.

quiz.q: Aisha's customers keep asking if her plantain flour tastes bitter. In copywriting terms, this is:
options: A desire
A feature
A call to action
An objection
quiz.explain: An objection is a reason a customer might not buy. Answering it in the copy, for example 'smooth, not bitter', removes a barrier.

quiz.q: A cake seller's delivery is late because of rain. Which tone is best?
options: Playful, with a joke about the weather
Calm and direct, with the reason, new time and a goodwill gesture
Formal, with no apology
Silent until the customer complains
quiz.explain: Serious moments need a calm, respectful tone that explains what happened and what happens next. Her voice can still be warm.

quiz.q: A seller posts 'Only 3 left!' every day for two months on the same product. What is the problem?
options: Scarcity should always be used
The message is too short
It is false scarcity, which breaks trust and may be misleading
She should say 'Only 2 left' instead
quiz.explain: Scarcity only works honestly when it is true. Repeating a false limit is misleading and customers soon notice.

modules.title: Core Copy Formats
modules.overview: Most small business selling happens in four short formats: the headline or first line, the product description, the social media caption and the call to action. This module gives you tested structures for each one, with many before-and-after rewrites from Nigerian businesses.

lessons.title: Headlines and first lines that stop the scroll
objectives: Explain why the first line decides whether the rest is read
Write headlines using six proven patterns
Check a headline against the 4 U's: useful, urgent, unique, ultra-specific
Write ten headline options and pick the strongest

blocks.text: On a phone, most people see only your first line, the picture and maybe the price before deciding whether to keep reading. On Instagram, a long caption is cut off after the first line or two with a 'more' link. On WhatsApp status, people tap past in a second. So the **headline**, meaning the title or first line, is the most important part of your copy. If it fails, nothing else gets read.

A good headline does one of three things for the right reader: it names her problem, promises a clear benefit, or makes her curious in a way that is relevant to the product. It does not need to be clever. Clear beats clever almost every time.

blocks.name: mobile-feed
blocks.alt: A person scrolling a social media feed on a phone
blocks.caption: Your first line competes with everything else in her feed, so it must speak to her straight away.

blocks.text: Six headline patterns that work

head: Pattern
Structure
Example
rows: How to keep your jollof from burning at the bottom
A question the right reader answers 'yes' to
Does your weave start shedding after two weeks?
3 signs your generator needs servicing before it breaks
Fresh, ready-to-cook vegetables at your door every Saturday
Now delivering to Gwarinpa and Kubwa
A real customer's line, with permission
'My son wore these shoes the whole term,' says Funmi

blocks.text: The 4 U's check
Copywriters often test headlines with the **4 U's**. A strong headline is usually high on at least two or three of them.

items: **Useful:** does it promise something the reader values?
**Urgent:** is there a real reason to read or act now (a date, a season, a stock limit)?
**Unique:** does it say something your competitors are not saying?
**Ultra-specific:** does it include details such as numbers, places, times or sizes?

blocks.title: The 4 U's headline check
items: Useful to the reader
Urgent for a real reason
Unique to your business
Ultra-specific with details
blocks.caption: Score each headline on these four; rewrite any that scores on only one.

blocks.title: Worked example: improving a laundry service headline
blocks.context: For example, Chioma runs a laundry and ironing service in Enugu for working people and students.
steps: Before: 'Best Laundry Services in Town.' Useful? Vaguely. Urgent? No. Unique? No, every laundry says this. Specific? No.
She adds a specific benefit: 'Your clothes washed, ironed and delivered in 48 hours.'
She adds the place and who it is for: 'Busy in Enugu? Your clothes washed, ironed and delivered in 48 hours.'
She adds an honest urgency for the season: 'Resumption week: drop off by Thursday, wear crisp uniforms on Monday.'
She now has two strong options to test on different days.
blocks.result: The new headlines score on useful, specific and, in one case, urgent. They tell the reader exactly what she gets and when, which 'Best Laundry Services in Town' never did.

blocks.text: Write ten, choose one

Professional copywriters rarely use their first headline. They write many and choose. Try this: set a timer for ten minutes and write ten headlines for the same product, using at least four different patterns from the table. Then cross out any that are vague, any you could not prove, and any that sound like every other seller. Read the last two or three aloud and pick the one that sounds most like a helpful friend.

blocks.title: Worked example: ten headlines for solar lanterns
blocks.context: For example, Kemi sells rechargeable solar lanterns in Ibadan. Her old first line was 'Solar lanterns now available.'
steps: How-to: 'How to light your shop all evening without buying fuel.'
Question: 'Tired of buying candles every time light goes?'
Number: '3 reasons traders in Bodija market are switching to solar lanterns.' (She only uses this if it is true that her Bodija customers are doing so.)
Direct benefit: 'Charge it in the sun by day, light your stall by night.'
News: 'New stock: solar lanterns with a phone charging port.'
She crosses out the vague ones and picks 'Charge it in the sun by day, light your stall by night' for her market trader customers.
blocks.result: The chosen headline is simple, specific and shows the benefit in one picture. She keeps the question version to test later on her status.

blocks.title: Avoid clickbait
blocks.text: A headline that promises something the post does not deliver, such as 'You won't believe this price' followed by a normal price, makes people feel tricked. They stop trusting your next post.

Keep the headline short enough to read in one glance on a phone, and let a second line, the **subheadline**, carry supporting detail. For example: headline 'Light your stall all evening without fuel', subheadline 'Solar lantern with phone charging port, about N12,000, delivered in Ibadan.' The headline earns attention; the subheadline earns trust.

blocks.title: Use numbers as digits
blocks.text: On small screens, '48 hours', 'N5,000' and '3 sizes' stand out more than 'forty-eight hours' or 'three sizes'. Digits catch the eye in a scroll.

takeaways: The first line decides whether the rest of your copy gets read
Clear beats clever: name the problem or promise a benefit
Use the six patterns and check headlines with the 4 U's
Write ten headlines and choose the best, never the first

activity.title: Ten headlines in ten minutes
steps: Choose one product or service.
Set a ten-minute timer and write ten headlines using at least four patterns.
Score each headline on the 4 U's (one point each).
Pick your top two and post them on different days with the same picture.
Record the views and replies for each.
activity.evidence: Your list of ten scored headlines and a note of the results for the two you posted

lessons.title: Product descriptions that turn features into benefits
objectives: Separate features from benefits for any product
Write a product description using a four-part structure
Include the practical details buyers need to decide
Adapt one description for WhatsApp catalogue, Instagram and an online store

blocks.text: A product description replaces you, the seller, when the customer cannot touch the product. In a shop she can feel the fabric, smell the cream and check the size. Online, your words and photos must do all of that. A weak description lists a few facts. A strong one helps her picture using the product and answers her doubts.
Features versus benefits, again and deeper

In Module 1 you learnt the 'which means' bridge. In product descriptions you need both sides: **benefits** to create desire and **features** to prove the benefits are real. Lead with the benefit, then support it with the feature.

blocks.title: Features prove, benefits sell
items: Features (facts)
Benefits (what she gets)
blocks.caption: Lead with the benefit on the right, then use the feature on the left as proof.

blocks.text: A four-part structure

items: **Hook line:** the main benefit for the main customer. 'A work dress that keeps you cool from morning meeting to evening traffic.'
**Benefits with proof:** two to four short lines, each a benefit linked to a feature.
**Practical details:** size, colour options, weight or quantity, ingredients or materials, care instructions, registration numbers where required, delivery time and price.
**Call to action:** how to order or what to send. 'Reply with your size and delivery area.'

blocks.name: label
blocks.caption: A good description answers every question a price tag cannot.

blocks.title: Worked example: a shea body butter, before and after
blocks.context: For example, Amaka makes whipped shea body butter in Abuja and sells 250g jars. Her catalogue description was very short.
steps: Before: 'Organic shea butter. Very good for skin. N4,500.'
Problems: 'organic' is a claim she cannot prove without certification; 'very good for skin' is vague; there are no details.
Hook: 'Soft, whipped shea butter that melts into dry skin without leaving you oily.'
Benefits with proof: 'Made with raw unrefined shea butter and coconut oil, so it absorbs quickly. Lightly scented with lemongrass. Whipped for 20 minutes so it spreads easily, even in harmattan.'
Details: '250g glass jar. Ingredients: shea butter, coconut oil, lemongrass essential oil. Store away from direct sun. Price: N4,500 (current price). Delivery within Abuja in 1 to 2 days.'
Action: 'Reply SHEA with your area to order.'
blocks.result: The new description removes the unprovable 'organic' claim, lists the real ingredients, explains why the texture is good and tells the buyer exactly how to order. If she sells a cosmetic widely, she also checks NAFDAC registration requirements and adds her number once she has it.

blocks.text: Use sensory and specific words

Help the buyer feel the product through her screen. Instead of 'nice', say what makes it nice: 'crunchy', 'buttery', 'soft like cotton wool', 'deep wine colour', 'smells like fresh lemongrass'. Instead of 'big', give a measurement or comparison: '45cm wide, fits a 15-inch laptop', 'feeds 4 adults'. Specific words build trust because they sound like someone who has really used the product.

head: Vague word
Specific replacement
rows: N2,500 for 12 pieces, about N210 each
5 litres, enough for a week of family cooking
Same-day delivery in Ikeja if you order before 12 noon
Ingredients: dried hibiscus, ginger, cloves, water

blocks.text: Adapt for each platform

items: **WhatsApp Business catalogue:** each item has a name, price, description and link. Put the hook and key details first, because people read on a small screen.
**Instagram post:** the hook goes in the first line of the caption; details can follow after line breaks.

**Online marketplace such as Jumia or your own Paystack or Selar store page:** buyers compare many listings, so put the most searched words (product type, size, colour) in the title and use bullet points for details.

blocks.title: Claims that need care
blocks.text: Do not claim a product cures, treats or prevents a disease unless it is approved for that purpose. Food, drinks, cosmetics and herbal products sold widely in Nigeria generally need NAFDAC registration, and health claims are closely controlled. Describe ingredients and use honestly instead.

blocks.title: Worked example: one description, three lengths
blocks.context: For example, Zainab sells a 1.5-litre electric kettle in Kano and needs a short, medium and long version of the same description. She checks every feature on the box before writing.
steps: Short (WhatsApp status, under 20 words): 'Hot water for tea without lighting the stove. 1.5-litre kettle, switches itself off. About N15,000. Reply KETTLE.'
Medium (WhatsApp catalogue): add the features that prove the benefits, taken from the box: stainless steel body, automatic switch-off when the water boils, and the warranty her shop actually offers.
Long (online store page): add the practical details: 1.5 litres, 220 to 240V, cable length, what is in the box, how to clean it, delivery areas and return policy.
She keeps the same hook in all three so the product is recognised wherever a buyer sees it.
blocks.result: Each platform gets the length it suits, but the core benefit and the facts never change, so the seller never contradicts herself.

blocks.text: Finally, update descriptions when something changes. If the price goes up or a colour sells out, change the listing the same day. An out-of-date description causes arguments and refunds.

takeaways: Lead with the benefit and use the feature as proof
Use four parts: hook, benefits with proof, practical details, call to action
Replace vague words with sensory, specific details
Never make health or 'organic' claims you cannot prove

activity.title: Rewrite three product descriptions
steps: Pick three products from your catalogue or price list.
For each one, list three features and turn them into benefits.
Rewrite each description using the four-part structure.
Replace every vague word with a specific detail or measurement.
Update your WhatsApp catalogue or store with the new descriptions.
activity.evidence: Screenshots of the three updated catalogue items, before and after

lessons.title: WhatsApp status and Instagram captions that get replies
objectives: Describe how WhatsApp status and Instagram captions differ
Write a status series that sells across a day
Structure an Instagram caption with hook, value, proof and call to action
Use hashtags, line breaks and emojis purposefully

blocks.text: For many Nigerian small businesses, WhatsApp status and Instagram are the shop window. The people viewing your status have already saved your number, so they know you. Instagram can reach new people through hashtags, the Explore page and shares. That difference changes how you write for each.

head: Feature
WhatsApp status
Instagram caption
rows: Contacts who saved your number (and whom your privacy settings allow)
Followers, plus new people through hashtags, Explore and shares
Stays on your profile unless you delete it
Short text on the image or a short text status
Up to 2,200 characters; only the start shows before 'more'
Like, comment, share, save or send a direct message
Daily offers, new stock, reminders, behind-the-scenes
Product showcases, tips, customer stories, brand building

blocks.name: social-media-post
blocks.alt: A woman preparing a social media post
blocks.caption: Status and captions work best when each post has one clear job.

blocks.text: Writing for WhatsApp status

items: Keep each status to one idea. If you have five products, use five statuses, not one crowded flyer.
Put a few big words on the picture (the benefit or price) and keep the rest for the caption box below it.
End with an action that uses the reply button: 'Reply 1 for small, 2 for big.'
Post a sequence rather than random posts, so the story builds through the day.

blocks.title: Worked example: a one-day status series for a small chops business
blocks.context: For example, Tolu sells small chops packs in Ibadan for parties and office events. Her old habit was to post one flyer with 12 items and the words 'Order now'.
steps: Status 1 (morning, photo of a packed tray): 'Planning a birthday or office party this weekend? 50 small chops packs ready in 24 hours.'
Status 2 (video of puff-puff being fried): 'Fresh, not reheated. We fry on the morning of your event.'
Status 3 (photo of the pack opened): 'Each pack: 4 puff-puff, 2 samosas, 2 spring rolls, 1 peppered chicken wing. About N2,000 per pack this month.'
Status 4 (screenshot of a customer message, shared with permission): 'Thank you, the guests finished everything!'
Status 5 (evening): 'I can take 3 more weekend orders. Reply PACK with the date and number of guests.'
blocks.result: Instead of one crowded flyer, the series gives attention, proof of freshness, clear contents and price, social proof, and an honest limit with a simple action. Each status can stand alone, but together they follow the AIDA order.

blocks.title: Instagram caption structure
items: Hook in first line
Value or story
Proof or details
One call to action
Relevant hashtags
blocks.caption: The hook earns the 'more' tap, and everything after it should lead to one action.

blocks.text: Writing Instagram captions

Because Instagram shows only the beginning of a caption, the first line must work like a headline. Use a question, a bold benefit or a surprising fact about the product. Then give value: a tip, a short story, how the product is made, or how to use it. Add proof or details, then one call to action. Short paragraphs with line breaks are easier to read on a phone than one long block.

blocks.title: Worked example: an Instagram caption for adire fabric
blocks.context: For example, Bisi sells hand-dyed adire fabric in Abeokuta and wants to reach buyers outside Ogun State.
steps: Before: 'New adire in stock. Nice colours. DM to buy. #adire #fabric #fashion #style #love #instagood'
Hook: 'Every piece of this indigo adire was tied and dyed by hand, so no two wrappers are exactly the same.'
Value: 'We fold, tie and dip each 2-yard piece several times in indigo to get this deep blue.'
Proof and details: 'Cotton, 2 yards per piece, about N8,000 each. Wash in cold water with mild soap to keep the colour rich. Shipping across Nigeria.'
Call to action: 'Send a DM with the word INDIGO and I will send photos of all 9 pieces available.'
Hashtags: '#adire #adirefabric #abeokuta #madeinnigeria #indigodye'
blocks.result: The new caption tells a story that makes the product special, gives care instructions and price, invites one action and uses specific hashtags that real buyers of adire are likely to search, instead of general ones like #love.

blocks.text: Hashtags, emojis and Pidgin

items: **Hashtags:** Instagram allows up to 30 per post. Use a handful of relevant, specific ones (product, place, style) rather than popular general tags.
**Emojis:** use them as signposts at the start of lines (a pin for location, a phone for ordering), not as decoration in every sentence.
**Pidgin and local languages:** a Pidgin or Yoruba hook can feel warm; keep price, size and ordering steps in clear words.

blocks.title: Write alt text
blocks.text: Instagram lets you add alt text, a short description of your image for people using screen readers. Describe the product plainly, for example 'Indigo adire wrapper folded on a wooden table'. It makes your shop more accessible.

takeaways: WhatsApp status reaches people who already know you; Instagram can reach new buyers
One idea per status, posted as a sequence through the day
Instagram captions need a headline-style first line, then value, proof and one action
Use specific hashtags and purposeful emojis, not decoration

activity.title: Plan a status series and one caption
steps: Choose one product and plan five statuses that follow attention, proof, details, social proof and action.
Write the text for each and post them across one day.
Write one Instagram caption for the same product using hook, value, proof, call to action and five specific hashtags.
Add alt text to the Instagram image.
Count the replies and messages you receive in 24 hours.
activity.evidence: Screenshots of your five statuses, your Instagram post and your reply count

lessons.title: Calls to action that make ordering easy
objectives: Write specific calls to action with a clear verb and next step
Remove friction from the ordering process
Create a WhatsApp click-to-chat link with a pre-filled message
Use honest urgency and reassurance near the call to action

blocks.text: A **call to action** (CTA) is the part of your copy that tells the reader exactly what to do next. It may be a sentence, a button or a link. Many good posts fail at this last step: the reader is interested, but the next step is unclear, slow or risky, so she does nothing.
What makes a strong call to action

items: **A clear action verb:** reply, send, book, tap, order, call, pay, register.
**One action, not five:** 'Call, DM, WhatsApp or visit our website' makes people hesitate. Choose the channel you respond to fastest.
**The exact next step:** what to send or where to tap. 'Reply with your size and area' is better than 'Contact us'.
**Low effort:** the fewer steps, the better. A word to reply with is easier than a form.
**A reason to act now, if it is true:** a deadline, limited stock or a delivery cut-off.

head: Weak call to action
Strong call to action
rows: Reply ORDER with your delivery area and I will send the total
Tap the link to see all 12 designs and prices
Order by Thursday 5pm for Saturday delivery
Pay with the secure Paystack link and get a receipt by email

blocks.name: click-here
blocks.alt: A hand pressing a large button on a screen
blocks.caption: A good call to action makes the next step feel small and obvious.

blocks.text: Remove friction

**Friction** is anything that makes the next step harder. Common friction points for Nigerian online buyers include not knowing the full price with delivery, not knowing how to pay, worrying about being scammed and waiting a long time for a reply. Your CTA and the text around it should remove as many of these as you can.

items: State the price and the delivery cost (or how it is calculated) before the CTA.
Say how payment works: transfer to a business account in your registered business name, a Paystack or Flutterwave payment link, a Moniepoint or Opay POS on delivery, or pay on delivery in some areas.
Add reassurance: your response time, return or exchange policy, or delivery tracking.
Make the channel one tap: a WhatsApp link, a 'Send message' button or a payment link.

blocks.text: Create a WhatsApp click-to-chat link

WhatsApp offers a free **click-to-chat** link. When someone taps it, a chat with you opens, even if they have not saved your number. You can add a pre-filled message so the customer only needs to press send. The format is https://wa.me/ followed by your full number in international format with no plus sign, zeros or dashes. To pre-fill text, add ?text= and your message, with spaces written as %20.

blocks.title: Worked example: building a click-to-chat link
blocks.context: For example, Grace sells grocery packs in Abuja. Her WhatsApp number is 0803 123 4567 (an illustrative number) and she wants the customer's first message to say 'Hello, I want a grocery pack'.
steps: Remove the first 0 and add Nigeria's country code 234: 2348031234567.
Start the link: https://wa.me/2348031234567
Add the message, replacing spaces with %20: ?text=Hello%2C%20I%20want%20a%20grocery%20pack (the comma becomes %2C).
Full link: https://wa.me/2348031234567?text=Hello%2C%20I%20want%20a%20grocery%20pack
She tests the link on her own phone before sharing it, then adds it to her Instagram bio and Facebook posts with the CTA 'Tap to order your pack on WhatsApp'.
blocks.result: Customers who tap the link land in a chat with the message already typed. Grace instantly knows what they want, and buyers do not need to save her number first.

blocks.title: Call to action checklist
items: One clear action verb
Exact next step stated
Price and delivery shown
Payment method explained
Honest reason to act now
blocks.caption: Check every CTA against this list before you post.

blocks.title: Protect your buyers and yourself
blocks.text: Ask customers to pay only into an account in your business or registered name, and never ask for card PINs, OTPs or passwords. Saying this in your copy reassures buyers who fear scams, and it protects you from impostors using your name.
Where to place the call to action

Put the main CTA at the end of your message, after the reader has the information she needs. In longer posts, product pages and emails, repeat the same CTA once near the top for people who are already convinced. On a picture flyer, the CTA and phone number should be big enough to read on a small phone screen without zooming. Never hide the ordering details in a comment or ask people to 'check the link in my bio' without saying what they will find there.

Finally, be ready for the response. A strong CTA that leads to a two-day wait for a reply wastes the sale. Use WhatsApp Business quick replies and greeting messages so customers get an instant first answer, and set aside times each day to respond fully.

takeaways: A call to action needs a clear verb, one channel and an exact next step
Remove friction by showing price, delivery and payment method
A wa.me click-to-chat link with pre-filled text makes ordering one tap
Only use urgency that is true, and reply quickly when people respond

activity.title: Build and test your ordering path
steps: Write your WhatsApp click-to-chat link with a pre-filled message for one product.
Test it on your own phone and a friend's phone.
Rewrite the CTA on three of your posts or catalogue items using the checklist.
Set up a WhatsApp Business greeting message or quick reply for new orders.
Ask a friend to 'buy' from you and note any step that confused them.
activity.evidence: Your working wa.me link, the three rewritten CTAs and your friend's feedback notes

quiz.q: Chioma's headline is 'Best Laundry Services in Town.' Using the 4 U's, what is its biggest weakness?
options: It is too specific
It is too urgent
It is vague and not unique; many laundries say the same
It is too long
quiz.explain: It is not specific, unique or urgent. Adding '48 hours', the city and the target reader made it stronger.

quiz.q: Amaka wants to describe her shea butter as 'organic' but has no certification. What should she do?
options: Remove the claim and list the real ingredients instead
Keep the word because customers like it
Write 'almost organic'
Put the word in capital letters
quiz.explain: A claim you cannot prove is misleading. Listing the actual ingredients is honest and still persuasive.

quiz.q: Which call to action creates the least friction?
options: Contact us for more information
Call, DM, email or visit our website
Patronise us today
Tap this link and send the pre-filled message to order
quiz.explain: It names one action, one channel and the exact next step, with the message already written for the buyer.

quiz.q: Grace's number is 0803 123 4567. What is the correct start of her click-to-chat link?
quiz.explain: Use the international format without the plus sign, the leading zero, spaces or dashes: 234 followed by 8031234567.

quiz.q: Which is the best first line for an Instagram caption selling hand-dyed adire?
options: New stock!!!
#adire #fashion #love
Every piece of this indigo adire was tied and dyed by hand, so no two are the same
DM to buy
quiz.explain: Only the first line shows before 'more', so it must work like a headline. This one gives a specific, appealing reason to read on.

modules.title: Sales Copy in Depth
modules.overview: Now you will write longer and more structured sales copy: paid Facebook and Instagram ads using the PAS framework, one-page sales pages, WhatsApp broadcast messages and email campaigns. Each lesson gives a structure, platform rules to respect and full before-and-after examples.

lessons.title: Facebook and Instagram ads with the PAS framework
objectives: Name the parts of a Meta ad and what each one is for
Write ad copy using Problem, Agitate, Solution (PAS)
Choose between PAS and AIDA for a given offer
Avoid copy that breaks Meta's advertising standards

blocks.text: Facebook and Instagram ads are both run through **Meta Ads Manager** (or the simpler 'Boost post' button). When you pay for an ad, your copy reaches people who do not know you yet. They did not choose to follow you, so your words must work harder and faster than on your WhatsApp status.
The parts of a Meta ad

head: Part
Where it appears
Its job
rows: The main message: hook, benefit, proof, action
Stop the scroll and show the product in use
Small text under the headline (not always shown)
Extra detail, such as delivery or price
Button such as Shop now, Learn more or Send WhatsApp message
Tell people what happens when they tap

blocks.text: Many Nigerian small businesses use **click-to-WhatsApp ads**, where the button opens a WhatsApp chat with the business. This suits sellers who close sales through conversation. The copy then needs to make people want to start that chat, and tell them what to ask for.

blocks.name: online-ad
blocks.alt: An online advertisement displayed on a screen
blocks.caption: A paid ad reaches strangers, so the copy must earn their attention in a second.

blocks.text: PAS: Problem, Agitate, Solution
**PAS** is a short framework that works well for ads because it starts where the reader is: with a problem.

items: **Problem:** name a specific problem your reader recognises.
**Agitate:** describe what that problem costs her: time, money, stress, embarrassment. Be honest and specific, not dramatic.
**Solution:** present your product as the way out, with proof and a call to action.

blocks.title: PAS framework
items: Problem: name it
Agitate: show the cost
Solution: your offer
Action: one next step
blocks.caption: PAS moves the reader from a problem she feels to a clear way out.

blocks.title: Worked example: PAS ad for a generator servicing business
blocks.context: For example, Uche runs a small generator repair and servicing workshop in Owerri and wants to run a click-to-WhatsApp ad to homeowners within his area.
steps: Before: 'We repair all kinds of generators. Call us today.'
Problem: 'Does your generator start, run for a few minutes, then go off?'

Agitate: 'You keep pulling the rope, food in the freezer starts to spoil and you end up buying fuel for a machine that will not stay on. Small faults like a dirty carburettor or a worn plug often get worse when ignored.'
Solution: 'We service petrol generators at your home in Owerri: carburettor cleaning, plug and oil change, and a full test run. Service from about N10,000 depending on the size of the generator.'
Action and button: 'Tap Send WhatsApp message and tell us your generator brand and size.'
Headline under the image: 'Home generator servicing in Owerri'
blocks.result: The ad speaks to a frustration the right reader feels strongly, explains the real cost of ignoring it, then offers a specific service with a starting price and a one-tap action. The agitation is factual, not frightening.

blocks.text: PAS or AIDA?

Use **PAS** when your product solves a clear, felt problem: repairs, pest control, hair loss products within legal claims, school fees savings plans, delivery services. Use **AIDA** when the product is more about desire than pain: fashion, cakes, décor, gifts, travel. Many good ads mix them, opening with a problem and then building desire.
Rules to respect

Meta reviews ads before they run and can reject them. Its Advertising Standards do not allow ads that assert or imply someone's personal attributes, such as health conditions, financial status or body shape. That changes how you write the Problem step.

head: Likely to be rejected
Better wording
rows: Are you fat? Lose belly fat fast!
Comfortable activewear for your morning walks
Are you broke? Make money now!
Learn bead-making as a skill you can sell
Unripe plantain flour: just dried unripe plantain, nothing added

blocks.title: Talk about the situation, not the person
blocks.text: 'Does your generator keep going off?' is about the generator. 'Are you poor?' is about the person. Describe situations and products, not people's bodies, health or money. Advertising in mainstream Nigerian media is also regulated by ARCON, the Advertising Regulatory Council of Nigeria, so check its rules if you grow into radio, TV or billboards.
Keep the primary text easy to scan

Only the first part of the primary text shows before a 'See more' link, so put the problem or main benefit in the opening line. Use short lines and one idea per line. Make the image do part of the work: a photo of the product being used by someone like your customer usually says more than text printed on the picture. If you include a price, make sure it matches what people will be charged when they message you.

Finally, write the ad to match where people land. If the button opens WhatsApp, have a greeting message ready. If it opens a page, the page headline should repeat the ad's promise so people know they are in the right place.

takeaways: A Meta ad has primary text, creative, headline, description and a CTA button
PAS: name the problem, show its real cost, offer the solution
Use PAS for felt problems and AIDA for desire-driven products
Describe situations, not people's bodies, health or money, to meet ad standards

activity.title: Write two ad versions
steps: Choose one product that solves a clear problem.
Write the primary text using PAS in four to six short lines.
Write a headline of no more than eight words and choose a CTA button.
Check every line against the 'situation, not the person' rule and rewrite anything that refers to a personal attribute.
Write a second version using AIDA so you can compare them later.
activity.evidence: Your two ad versions (PAS and AIDA) with headlines and chosen buttons

lessons.title: One-page sales pages and landing pages
objectives: Explain what a landing page is and when you need one
Plan a sales page using a proven section order
Write a headline, benefits, proof, offer and FAQ for one product
Choose a simple tool to publish a page

blocks.text: A **landing page** is a single web page built for one purpose: to get visitors to take one action, such as buying, registering or sending a message. A **sales page** is a longer landing page that sells a product or course. You need one when your offer needs more explanation than a caption allows, for example a training programme, a bulk catering package or a pre-order.
Unlike a full website with many menus, a landing page removes distractions. Every section leads to the same button.

blocks.name: landing-page
blocks.alt: A person designing a landing page layout
blocks.caption: A landing page has one job, and every section points to the same button.

blocks.text: A proven section order

items: **Headline and subheadline:** the main promise and who it is for. Repeat the promise from your ad or post.
**The problem:** a short paragraph showing you understand her situation.
**The solution and benefits:** what you offer and three to six benefits, each with a feature as proof.
**Proof:** real testimonials, photos of past work, numbers you can back up, your experience or registration.
**The offer:** exactly what she gets, the price, any bonus, the deadline if there is one.
**Reassurance:** guarantee or refund policy you can honour, delivery details, secure payment.
**Frequently asked questions:** answers to the main objections.
**Call to action:** a clear button, repeated after major sections.

blocks.title: Sales page from top to bottom
items: Headline and promise
Problem and solution
Benefits and proof
Offer and price
FAQ and guarantee
Call to action
blocks.caption: The page follows the order of the reader's questions, from 'is this for me?' to 'how do I pay?'

blocks.title: Worked example: a sales page for a baking class
blocks.context: For example, Funke runs weekend baking classes in Lagos and wants a page for her 4-week beginner class.
steps: Headline: 'Bake soft bread and cakes you can sell, in 4 Saturdays.'
Subheadline: 'A hands-on beginner class in Surulere for women who want to start a home baking business.'
Problem: 'You have watched many videos, but your cakes still sink and your bread comes out hard. And you are not sure how to price what you bake.'

Benefits with proof: 'Bake in our kitchen with your own hands, not just watch. Take home recipes for bread, sponge cake, chin chin and meat pie. Learn how to cost a recipe so you know your profit before you sell.'
Proof: three real student comments with their permission and first names, and photos of past classes.
Offer: 'Fee: N60,000 (current fee), ingredients included. 12 seats per class so everyone gets hands-on time. Next class starts 1st Saturday of the month.'
FAQ: 'Do I need an oven at home? What if I miss a Saturday? Can I pay in two parts?'
Call to action button: 'Reserve my seat' linking to a Paystack payment page.
blocks.result: The page answers every question a careful buyer would ask, in the order she would ask it. The 12-seat limit is true and explained, so it creates honest urgency.

blocks.text: Writing the benefits section

Use short bullet points that start with the result. Put the strongest benefit first and the most technical one last. Avoid stacking adjectives ('amazing, life-changing, premium'). One specific detail, such as 'take home 6 tested recipes', beats three adjectives.

head: Weak bullet
Strong bullet
rows: Bake 6 recipes yourself, from bread to meat pie
Taught by a baker who has run a home bakery for 8 years (only if true)
Learn to cost a recipe and set a selling price with profit
Get a certificate of attendance to show customers

blocks.text: Simple tools to publish a page

items: **Paystack Payment Pages** or Flutterwave payment links: a simple page with a description and a pay button.
**Selar:** a platform popular with African creators for selling courses, e-books and event tickets.
**Google Sites:** free, simple pages built with a Google account.
**Your WhatsApp Business catalogue link:** for product sellers, a shareable list of items with prices.

blocks.title: Design for phones first
blocks.text: Most of your visitors will be on a phone, often on costly mobile data. Use short paragraphs, compress your photos, put the button where a thumb can reach it, and preview the page on your own phone before sharing it.
Writing the FAQ section

The FAQ is where you handle objections calmly. Take the questions straight from your chats. Answer each in one to three sentences, and never dodge. If the honest answer is 'No, you need an oven at home to practise', say so and suggest what she can do instead. A direct answer to an uncomfortable question builds more trust than a page that pretends there are no downsides. Keep the most common question, often about price, payment in parts or refunds, at the top.

Before you share the page, read it as a stranger would. Could someone who has never heard of you understand the offer, believe it, and pay without asking a single question? If not, the missing answer belongs on the page.

takeaways: A landing page has one goal and removes distractions
Follow the reader's questions: promise, problem, benefits, proof, offer, FAQ, action
Benefit bullets start with the result and include one specific detail
Use simple tools like Paystack Payment Pages, Selar or Google Sites, and test on a phone

activity.title: Draft a one-page sales page
steps: Choose one offer that needs more explanation than a caption.
Write a headline and subheadline that state the promise and who it is for.
Write the problem paragraph, five benefit bullets and three FAQs.
Add your price, what is included and your refund or exchange policy.
Publish it with a free tool or write it in a document, and ask one person to read it and tell you what is unclear.
activity.evidence: The draft or live page and the reader's feedback

lessons.title: WhatsApp broadcast messages that people welcome
objectives: Explain how WhatsApp broadcast lists work and their limits
Get customers' permission before adding them to a list
Write broadcast messages for new stock, offers and reminders
Plan a sending rhythm that keeps people from muting or blocking you

blocks.text: A **broadcast list** in WhatsApp lets you send one message to many contacts at once. Each person receives it as a private message from you, and their reply comes back to you privately. Nobody sees who else is on the list. This makes broadcasts feel personal, which is why they are powerful, and also why badly written ones feel like spam.
How broadcast lists work

items: Only contacts who have **saved your number** in their phone receive your broadcast. If someone has not saved you, the message will not reach them.
Each list has a limit on the number of contacts (it has long been 256 per list; check the current limit in your app).
You can create several lists, for example 'Wholesale buyers', 'Lagos retail' and 'Abuja retail'.
In the WhatsApp Business app you can also use **labels** to group chats, **quick replies** for common answers, a **catalogue** for your products, and greeting and away messages.
Businesses that need to message very large numbers of people use the WhatsApp Business Platform through an approved provider, which has its own rules on opt-in and message templates.

blocks.name: message-sent
blocks.alt: A person sending a message from a phone
blocks.caption: A broadcast arrives like a personal message, so it should read like one.

blocks.text: Permission first

Ask before you add someone to a broadcast list, and make it easy to leave. This is good manners, it keeps people from blocking or reporting you, and it respects Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023, which expects a lawful basis such as consent when you use people's contact details for marketing.

blocks.title: Worked example: asking permission
blocks.context: For example, Ifeoma sells wholesale and retail fabrics in Aba. After every sale she wants to invite buyers to her new-stock list.
steps: Before: she added every customer's number to a broadcast list without asking. Some replied 'Who is this?' and some blocked her.

After a sale, she now sends: 'Thank you for your order, Chika. I send new fabric arrivals about once a week, with prices. Would you like to receive them? Reply YES to join, and you can reply STOP any time.'
She saves the customer's number, adds those who reply YES to the right list and labels them in WhatsApp Business.
She reminds new subscribers to save her number so the broadcasts reach them.
blocks.result: Her list is smaller but everyone on it wants her messages, so more people open and reply. Very few people block her.

blocks.text: Structure of a good broadcast

items: **Personal opening:** a short greeting. Avoid 'Dear valued customer'.
**One main point:** new stock, a restock, an offer, a reminder or a useful tip. Not all of them at once.
**Key details:** price, sizes, quantities, deadline.
**One simple action:** a word to reply with, or a link.
**Easy exit:** occasionally remind people they can reply STOP.

blocks.title: Worked example: a restock broadcast, before and after
blocks.context: For example, Ifeoma has just restocked a popular lace that sold out last month.
steps: Before: 'DEAR VALUED CUSTOMERS!!! NEW GOODS HAVE ARRIVED!!! ALL KINDS OF LACE, ANKARA, GEORGE, ASO OKE. COME AND BUY. PRICES ARE VERY CHEAP!!!'

After: 'Good morning. The wine Swiss lace that sold out last month is back. 5 yards for about N38,000. I have 14 pieces, and 6 are already reserved. Reply WINE to reserve one. Photos and close-up video below.'
She follows with one short video showing the lace in daylight.
blocks.result: The new message is calm, specific and personal, with real stock numbers and one action. The capital letters and vague 'all kinds' list are gone.

blocks.title: A healthy broadcast rhythm
items: Ask permission
Send useful message
Reply to responses
Check who opted out
Improve next message
blocks.caption: Each broadcast should teach you something that makes the next one better.

blocks.text: How often to send

There is no single correct number. Many small sellers find that one to two broadcasts a week, sent at a time customers are free, works better than daily messages. Watch the signs: if replies drop or people ask to leave, you are sending too often or the messages are not useful. Mix sales messages with helpful ones, such as how to care for a fabric or what to wear to an owambe this season.

head: Message type
Example first line
rows: Good morning. The wine Swiss lace is back in stock.
Quick tip: wash ankara inside out in cold water to keep the colour.
This week only, free delivery in Aba on orders above N50,000.
A reminder: reserved pieces are held until 6pm today.

blocks.title: Protect customers from scams
blocks.text: Scammers sometimes copy a seller's name and photo. Tell your list which account number you use and that you will never ask for card PINs or OTPs. Send payment details only after a customer has confirmed an order with you.

takeaways: Broadcasts reach only people who have saved your number
Ask permission before adding anyone and make leaving easy
Each broadcast should have one point, real details and one action
Send at a steady, moderate rhythm and mix offers with useful tips

activity.title: Start a permission-based broadcast list
steps: Write a short permission message and send it to 10 recent customers.
Create a broadcast list with those who reply YES and label them in WhatsApp Business.
Write one broadcast using the five-part structure.
Send it at a time your customers are free and record the replies.
Note one change you will make for the next broadcast.
activity.evidence: Screenshot of your permission message, your broadcast and a note of the replies

lessons.title: Email campaigns: subject lines, body copy and consent
objectives: Write subject lines and preview text that get emails opened
Structure a sales email around one goal
Plan a short email sequence for a launch or offer
Follow consent and unsubscribe rules

blocks.text: Email may feel old-fashioned next to WhatsApp, but it is still important for businesses that sell to professionals, organisations, diaspora customers and people who buy online courses or services. You own your email list, unlike your followers on a social platform. If an account is restricted, your email list still works.
Three things people see before they open

items: **Sender name:** use a real name people recognise, for example 'Amaka from Shea by Amaka', rather than 'info' or 'noreply'.
**Subject line:** the headline of your email. Short, specific and honest.

**Preview text:** the line that shows after the subject in many inboxes. If you do not set it, the inbox shows the first words of your email, which may be 'View in browser'. Most email tools let you write it.

blocks.name: email-campaign
blocks.alt: A person sending an email campaign to many recipients
blocks.caption: In email, the sender name, subject line and preview text decide whether the rest is read.

head: Weak subject line
Stronger subject line
rows: 3 ways to keep your shea butter from going grainy
Your 10% discount ends Friday at midnight
Funke, your baking class seat is saved until Thursday
New delivery days for Abuja from Monday

blocks.text: One email, one goal

Each sales email should have one goal: to get a click to the sales page, a reply, a booking or a payment. Write it like a letter to one person. Short paragraphs, a friendly opening, the main message, and one button or link repeated at most twice. A **P.S.** at the end is often read, so use it to repeat the deadline or main benefit.

blocks.title: Worked example: a launch email for a catering package
blocks.context: For example, Ruth runs a catering business in Abuja and is launching office lunch packages for companies with 10 or more staff.
steps: Before: subject 'Ruth's Kitchen Update', body a long list of every dish she makes, with no price and no clear next step.
Subject: 'Hot office lunches for your team, delivered by 12:30'
Preview text: 'Weekly packages for teams of 10 or more in Abuja.'
Opening: 'Hello Tunde, many office managers tell me lunch orders take up their whole morning.'

Main message: 'Our weekly lunch package delivers hot meals to your office every working day by 12:30pm. Your staff choose from 3 meals a day by WhatsApp, and you get one invoice at the end of the week.'
Offer: 'Packages from about N3,500 per person per day for teams of 10 or more (current pricing). The first day is a free tasting for up to 10 people.'
Call to action: a button 'Book a free tasting day' and a P.S.: 'Tasting days for October are limited to 8 companies, because we deliver everything ourselves.'
blocks.result: The email is addressed to one person's problem, explains how the service works, gives a starting price and a low-risk first step, and closes with an honest limit.

blocks.text: A simple three-email sequence

blocks.title: Three-email launch sequence
items: Day 1: announce and explain
Day 3: proof and FAQ
Last day: honest reminder
blocks.caption: A short sequence gives busy readers more than one chance to act, without flooding their inbox.

items: **Email 1, announcement:** what it is, who it is for, the main benefit and the deadline.
**Email 2, proof and questions:** a customer story, photos and answers to the top three objections.
**Email 3, reminder:** short, friendly reminder that the offer or registration closes today.

blocks.text: Consent and unsubscribe

Only email people who agreed to hear from you, for example by ticking a box on your sign-up form or asking to join. Never buy email lists. Every marketing email should include a clear unsubscribe link, which email tools such as Mailchimp, Brevo and MailerLite add automatically. Large inbox providers like Gmail and Yahoo now expect bulk senders to make unsubscribing easy, and emails that people mark as spam reduce the chance your future emails reach anyone's inbox.
Make the email easy to read on a phone

items: Keep paragraphs to two or three short sentences.
Use one simple layout. A plain, letter-style email often feels more personal than a heavily designed one.
Make the button big and the button text specific: 'Book a free tasting day' rather than 'Click here'.
Add your business name, address or phone number at the bottom so readers know who you are.
Send a test to yourself and read it on your phone before sending to your list.

blocks.text: After sending, look at three numbers in your email tool: how many people opened, how many clicked the link and how many unsubscribed. Opens tell you about the subject line, clicks tell you about the body and the call to action, and a jump in unsubscribes tells you the email was not welcome.

blocks.title: Start small
blocks.text: Several email tools offer free plans for small lists; check each tool's current limits. Start by collecting emails from customers who buy online or attend your classes, with their permission, and send one genuinely useful email a month.

takeaways: The sender name, subject line and preview text decide whether an email is opened
Each sales email has one goal and one main link or button
A short sequence of announcement, proof and reminder gives readers time to act
Email only people who agreed, and always include an unsubscribe link

activity.title: Write a three-email sequence
steps: Choose one offer with a real deadline or limited places.
Write a subject line and preview text for each of the three emails.
Write the body of email 1 with one goal, one button and a P.S.
Outline emails 2 and 3 using the proof-and-FAQ and reminder structure.
Send email 1 to yourself and check how it looks on your phone.
activity.evidence: Your three subject lines, preview texts, the full first email and a screenshot of it on your phone

quiz.q: Uche writes an ad starting 'Does your generator start, run for a few minutes, then go off?' Which PAS step is this?
options: Agitate
Problem
Solution
Proof
quiz.explain: The first step of PAS names a specific problem the reader recognises. Agitate comes next, showing what the problem costs.

quiz.q: Which ad opening is most likely to break Meta's rule on personal attributes?
options: Comfortable activewear for morning walks
Is your freezer full of spoilt food when light goes?
Are you overweight? Lose belly fat fast!
Fresh bread delivered every morning
quiz.explain: It asserts something about the reader's body. Meta's standards do not allow ads that assert or imply personal attributes such as health or body shape.

quiz.q: Ifeoma's broadcast is not reaching some customers. What is the most likely reason?
options: Those customers have not saved her number
Her messages are too short
She used a label
She sent it in the morning
quiz.explain: WhatsApp broadcasts are delivered only to contacts who have saved your number in their phone.

quiz.q: Funke's sales page says '12 seats per class so everyone gets hands-on time.' Why is this good copy?
options: It hides the price
