It creates honest urgency and explains the reason
It replaces the need for testimonials
It makes the page longer
quiz.explain: A true limit with a reason behind it is honest scarcity. Customers believe it because they understand why it exists.

quiz.q: Ruth's email subject is 'Ruth's Kitchen Update'. Which change would most likely improve opens?
options: Add three exclamation marks
Change the sender name to noreply
Write it in capital letters
Make it specific: 'Hot office lunches for your team, delivered by 12:30'
quiz.explain: A specific subject line tells the reader what is in it for them. Capitals, exclamation marks and 'noreply' senders reduce trust.

quiz.q: Which is the best way to build an email list?
options: Buy a list of 10,000 Nigerian emails
Copy emails from a WhatsApp group
Invite customers to sign up with a clear tick box and an unsubscribe option
Add every business card you collect without asking
quiz.explain: Consent is the right basis for marketing emails, and willing subscribers open and buy more. Bought or copied lists lead to spam complaints.

modules.title: Advanced Copy Skills
modules.overview: The last module makes your copy more believable and more effective over time. You will tell true customer stories, answer objections and use testimonials ethically, write web copy that people can find on Google, and edit and A/B test your copy so you learn what your customers respond to.

lessons.title: Storytelling in sales copy: before, after and the bridge
objectives: Explain why stories make sales copy more believable
Write a short story using Before, After, Bridge (BAB)
Tell a founder story and a customer story honestly
Choose specific details that make a story feel real

blocks.text: People remember stories more easily than lists of features. A story lets the reader see someone like herself facing a problem and finding a way through. It also carries proof in a natural way: instead of saying 'our tutoring works', you show one child's journey from struggling to confident.

In sales copy, the customer is the hero of the story, not your business. Your product is the helper or tool that makes the change possible. When sellers make themselves the hero ('We are the best, we have won awards'), readers lose interest. When the reader sees herself in the hero, she leans in.

blocks.name: book-writer
blocks.alt: A woman writing a story in a notebook
blocks.caption: A short, true story often persuades more than a long list of features.

blocks.text: Before, After, Bridge (BAB)

items: **Before:** the situation and frustration before the product.
**After:** what life looks like once the problem is solved.
**Bridge:** how the product or service got her from before to after, and how the reader can do the same.

blocks.title: Before, After, Bridge
items: Before: the struggle
After: the better situation
Bridge: how she got there
blocks.caption: Show the contrast first, then reveal the bridge that connects the two.

blocks.title: Worked example: a BAB story for a home tutoring service
blocks.context: For example, Esther runs after-school maths tutoring in Benin City. A parent agreed that his daughter's story could be shared using her first name.
steps: Before: 'In January, Osaro dreaded maths homework. She would sit at the table for an hour and finish two questions, and her mum had to beg her to try.'
After: 'By the end of the term, she was finishing her homework before dinner and asked for extra fractions practice.'
Bridge: 'What changed? Two evenings a week, we went back to the basics she had missed, used objects and drawings for fractions, and gave her small wins every session.'
Call to action: 'We have 4 places left for this term in GRA and Ugbowo. Reply MATHS and I will tell you how the first free assessment works.'
blocks.result: The story shows a believable change with specific details (two questions in an hour, fractions, two evenings a week) instead of claiming 'excellent results'. It ends with a clear, low-risk next step. It does not promise that every child will improve in the same way.

blocks.text: Three stories every small business can tell

head: Story type
What it shows
Example opening
rows: Proof that the product works for people like the reader
'When Halima first ordered, she only wanted one tray for her son's naming...'
Why you started and why you care
'I started making pap at home because I could not find one my children would eat...'
How it is made, what makes it special
'Each basket takes our weavers in Oyo about two days...' (only if true)

blocks.text: Specific details make stories believable

Compare 'Our customers love our cakes' with 'Last Saturday, a mother in Ikorodu sent me a voice note at 11pm saying the children had eaten the cake before the photos were taken.' The second feels real because it includes a day, a place, a person and a small surprising detail. Use details you actually know. If you do not remember them, ask the customer, or tell a smaller story you do know well.

blocks.title: Worked example: a founder story for a pap business
blocks.context: For example, Nkechi makes and sells fermented pap (ogi) in Enugu in hygienic packs.
steps: Before: 'We are the best pap producer in Enugu. Our pap is very hygienic. Order now.'

She rewrites it as a founder story: 'When my first child started eating solid food, I wanted pap I could trust. I watched how my mother soaked, ground and sieved the corn, and I learnt to do it in a clean kitchen with filtered water.'
She adds the bridge to the customer: 'Today I make the same pap for other mothers, sealed in 1kg packs, so you get the taste of home-made ogi without the soaking and sieving.'
She adds proof and action: 'See how we make it in the video. Reply OGI to order for delivery in Enugu.'
blocks.result: The story replaces empty claims ('best', 'very hygienic') with a believable reason she cares about cleanliness and a picture of how it is made. Note that she does not claim health benefits she cannot prove.

blocks.title: Never invent a story
blocks.text: A made-up customer story is a fake testimonial, even if it sounds realistic. Use real stories with permission, change or remove names if the customer prefers, and never exaggerate results.

Keep stories short in captions and statuses: three to five sentences is often enough. Save longer stories for landing pages, emails and video. You can also tell a story across several WhatsApp statuses in one day, one stage per status.

takeaways: In sales stories, the customer is the hero and your product is the helper
BAB: show the before, show the after, then reveal the bridge
Specific, true details make stories believable
Use real stories with permission and never invent results

activity.title: Write one customer story and one founder story
steps: Ask one happy customer if you may share their experience and how they would like to be named.
Write their story using Before, After, Bridge in five sentences or fewer.
Write your own founder story in five sentences or fewer, ending with a link to what you sell.
Underline every specific detail. Add one more if the story feels general.
Post one of the stories and note the replies.
activity.evidence: Both written stories, the customer's permission message and a screenshot of the posted story

lessons.title: Handling objections and using testimonials ethically
objectives: List the common objections Nigerian online buyers raise
Answer objections in your copy before they are asked
Collect and use testimonials with permission and honesty
Write guarantees and policies you can actually honour

blocks.text: An **objection** is a reason a customer hesitates. In face-to-face selling, she tells you and you answer. Online, she simply scrolls away. Good copy answers the main objections in advance, so the buyer's doubts are settled before she leaves.
Common objections and how copy answers them

head: Objection
What she is thinking
How your copy can answer
rows: Will I pay and receive nothing?
Business name and address, real reviews, account in business name, pay on delivery option where possible
What I ordered vs what I got
Will it look like the picture?
Real photos and videos in daylight, measurements, exchange policy
Show value: cost per use, what is included, quality details; offer a smaller size
Delivery areas, times and fees stated clearly
Size guide, who it is for and who it is not for
An honest deadline or reason to act now

blocks.name: testimonials
blocks.alt: Customer testimonial cards with star ratings
blocks.caption: Real words from real customers answer the trust objection better than any claim you make about yourself.

blocks.title: Worked example: answering the price objection
blocks.context: For example, Sade sells handmade leather sandals in Ibadan at about N25,000 a pair. Many people reply 'too expensive'.
steps: Before: 'Original leather sandals. N25,000. No price negotiation.'
She breaks down the value: 'Full cow leather upper and a stitched sole, not glued, so it does not peel after rainy season.'

She shows cost over time: 'If a pair lasts you two years of regular wear, that is about N1,050 a month.' She only says this because her past customers report this kind of wear; otherwise she would leave it out.
She addresses fit: 'Send your foot length in cm and I will confirm your size before you pay.'
She offers an option: 'Prefer something lighter on the pocket? Our slip-on style is about N15,000.'
blocks.result: Instead of arguing about price, the copy explains why the sandals cost what they cost, reduces the risk of the wrong size and offers a cheaper choice. Some buyers will still say no, and that is fine.

blocks.text: Testimonials: powerful and easy to misuse

A **testimonial** is a customer's own words about your product. It is one of the strongest forms of social proof because it comes from someone who is not the seller. That is exactly why fake or misleading testimonials are so damaging, and why consumer protection rules in many countries treat them seriously. In Nigeria, the FCCPC enforces law against misleading representations to consumers.

blocks.title: Ethical versus unethical testimonials
items: Ethical
Unethical
blocks.caption: If a testimonial would mislead a reasonable buyer, do not use it.

items: **Ask for permission** in writing, for example on WhatsApp: 'May I share your message on my status, with your first name only?'
**Keep their meaning.** You may shorten a testimonial or fix a spelling mistake, but do not change what they said or add claims.
**Hide private details** such as phone numbers, profile photos and other chats in any screenshot.
**Disclose connections.** If you gave someone a free product or payment for a review, say so, for example 'received a free sample'.
**Do not present unusual results as typical,** especially for skin, hair, weight or income products.
**Never write reviews yourself** or ask friends to post reviews for products they have not used.

blocks.text: Guarantees and policies you can keep

A clear policy removes risk for the buyer: 'Exchange within 3 days if the size is wrong, item unused and with tags.' Only promise what you can afford to honour. A generous policy you break is worse than a modest one you keep. Write the conditions plainly so there is no argument later.

blocks.title: Worked example: turning a messy screenshot into an ethical testimonial
blocks.context: For example, Sade receives this WhatsApp message from a customer named Yetunde: 'Omo these sandals are sweet!! Wore them to my cousin's wedding and danced all night, no pain. My sister wants one too, abeg send price.'
steps: She asks: 'Thank you, Yetunde! May I share your message on my status and page, with your first name only?' Yetunde replies 'Yes, no problem.'
She keeps Yetunde's words and meaning but removes the line asking for a price, which is not part of the review.
In the screenshot, she covers the phone number and profile photo.
Final testimonial: 'Wore them to my cousin's wedding and danced all night, no pain.' Yetunde, Ibadan.
She saves the permission message in a 'Testimonials' label in WhatsApp Business in case anyone asks.
blocks.result: The testimonial is real, specific, shared with permission and free of private details. It answers the comfort objection in a customer's own voice, which is more believable than Sade saying 'very comfortable'.

blocks.title: Who it is not for
blocks.text: Saying who your product is not for builds trust. 'These sandals are not for wide feet; try our slip-on style instead' tells the buyer you care about the right fit, not just a sale.

takeaways: Answer the main objections in your copy before buyers have to ask
Show value, reduce risk and offer options instead of arguing about price
Use testimonials only with permission, keep their meaning and disclose any gifts
Promise only guarantees and policies you can honour

activity.title: Build an objection and proof bank
steps: List the five objections you hear most often, using customers' own words.
Write a one- or two-sentence answer for each that you can add to posts or your FAQ.
Ask three happy customers for permission to share their feedback, and how to name them.
Prepare their testimonials with private details hidden.
Write your exchange or refund policy in three plain sentences.
activity.evidence: Your objection and answer list, three permission messages, and your written policy

lessons.title: Writing for Google search without losing the human
objectives: Explain in plain words how search engine optimisation (SEO) helps buyers find you
Find the words local customers type into Google
Write a page title, meta description and headings for a product or service page
Set up a Google Business Profile description that sells

blocks.text: **Search engine optimisation (SEO)** means making your web pages easy for search engines like Google to understand and show to the right people. When someone types 'cake delivery in Lekki' or 'tailor near Wuse market', Google tries to show the most helpful results. Your copy can help you appear there.

Google's own guidance tells site owners to create helpful, reliable content written for people first, not to stuff pages with keywords. Good SEO copy is simply good sales copy that uses the words customers search with.

blocks.name: search-engines
blocks.alt: A person using a search engine on a large screen
blocks.caption: When your page uses the words customers type, Google can match it to their search.

blocks.text: Find the words customers use

items: Type your product and town into Google and note the suggestions that appear as you type (autocomplete).
Look at the 'People also ask' questions on the results page.
Note the words customers use in your chats: do they say 'small chops' or 'finger foods', 'aso ebi' or 'party fabric'?
If you have a Google Ads account, the free Keyword Planner shows rough search interest for words.
Choose one main phrase per page, such as 'small chops delivery in Ibadan', plus a few related phrases.

blocks.text: Where the words go

head: Page element
What it is
Tip
rows: The clickable blue line Google often shows in results
Include the main phrase and your brand; keep it short and descriptive
A short summary Google sometimes shows under the title
Write it like an ad: benefit, place, reason to click
The big heading at the top of the page
Say clearly what the page offers
Answer questions fully, mention your area naturally
Describe the image plainly, for accessibility and search

blocks.title: From search to sale
items: Customer searches a phrase
Your title matches it
Description earns the click
Page answers her questions
She contacts or pays
blocks.caption: SEO gets the click, but sales copy on the page still has to win the order.

blocks.title: Worked example: a catering service page
blocks.context: For example, Bukola runs a small chops and party catering business in Ibadan and has a simple website page that nobody finds.
steps: Before title: 'Home'. Before heading: 'Welcome to Bukky's Kitchen!!!'
She checks Google autocomplete and sees phrases like 'small chops in Ibadan' and 'small chops price list'.
New title: 'Small Chops Delivery in Ibadan | Bukky's Kitchen'
New meta description: 'Fresh small chops packs for parties and offices in Ibadan. Fried on the day, delivered on time. See our price list and order on WhatsApp.'
New H1: 'Small chops for parties and offices in Ibadan'
New subheadings: 'What is in each pack?', 'Small chops price list', 'Which areas do you deliver to?', 'How do I order?'
blocks.result: The page now uses the words people actually search, tells Google and readers what it offers and where, and answers the common questions on the page. It still sounds human, not stuffed with keywords.

blocks.text: Google Business Profile

For local businesses, a free **Google Business Profile** can matter as much as a website. It shows your business on Google Maps and in local search results with your address, opening hours, phone number, photos and reviews. Write the business description like good sales copy: what you offer, for whom, where, and what makes you different. Keep it factual; do not stuff it with keywords or include links and promotions in the description.

blocks.title: Do not keyword-stuff
blocks.text: Repeating 'small chops Ibadan, best small chops Ibadan, cheap small chops Ibadan' over and over makes the page unpleasant to read. Google's spam policies treat keyword stuffing as a bad practice. Write naturally for the customer.

blocks.title: Worked example: a Google Business Profile description
blocks.context: For example, Rakiya runs a tailoring shop near Wuse Market in Abuja and wants local customers to find her on Google Maps.
steps: Before: 'Best tailor in Abuja!!! We sew everything. Fast fast. Call now. Visit www... for promo!!!'
She removes the 'best' claim, the shouting, the link and the promotion, which do not belong in the description.

After: 'Ladies' and men's tailoring near Wuse Market, Abuja. We sew native attire, office wear, aso ebi and alterations from your fabric or ours. Most outfits are ready in 5 to 7 working days, and express sewing is available. Walk in for measurements Monday to Saturday.'
She checks that her opening hours, phone number and map pin are correct, and adds clear photos of finished outfits.
blocks.result: The description tells a searcher exactly what Rakiya sews, where, how long it takes and what to do next, in plain words that also match what people type, such as 'tailor near Wuse Market'.

blocks.text: SEO takes time. A new page may take weeks to appear in results. Keep your details correct, add helpful pages that answer real questions, and ask happy customers to leave honest Google reviews.

takeaways: SEO helps people searching on Google find your pages
Use the words customers actually type, found through autocomplete and your chats
Put the main phrase in the title, meta description and main heading, naturally
A complete Google Business Profile helps local buyers find you

activity.title: Optimise one page or profile
steps: Search Google for your main product and town and write down five phrases from autocomplete and 'People also ask'.
Choose one main phrase for your page.
Write a new title, meta description, H1 and three question subheadings.
Write or improve your Google Business Profile description.
Ask two happy customers to leave an honest Google review.
activity.evidence: Your phrase list, new page elements and a screenshot of your Google Business Profile

lessons.title: Editing your copy and A/B testing what works
objectives: Edit a draft using a clear checklist
Cut unnecessary words and replace vague ones
Run a fair A/B test that changes one thing at a time
Record results in a simple sheet and decide what to keep

blocks.text: Good copy is rarely written; it is rewritten. Your first draft gets the ideas down. Editing makes it clear, short and persuasive. Testing then shows you which version your customers actually prefer, so you stop guessing.
A seven-point editing checklist

items: **Reader:** is it clearly written for one type of customer?
**First line:** would she stop scrolling for it?
**Benefits:** does every feature have a 'which means'?
**Specifics:** have you replaced vague words with numbers, places and details?
**Proof:** is there at least one reason to believe you?
**Action:** is there one clear call to action with the exact next step?
**Truth:** is every claim true and can you prove it?

blocks.name: split-testing
blocks.alt: Two versions of a design being compared side by side
blocks.caption: A/B testing compares two versions so your customers' responses, not your guesses, decide.

blocks.text: Cut, simplify, read aloud

items: Cut filler words: 'very', 'really', 'in order to', 'we wish to inform you that'.
Use short words: 'use' not 'utilise', 'buy' not 'purchase', 'help' not 'facilitate'.
Keep most sentences short. One idea per sentence.
Read your copy aloud. Wherever you stumble or run out of breath, rewrite.
Free tools such as the Hemingway Editor highlight long, hard sentences.

blocks.title: Worked example: editing a caption
blocks.context: For example, Hauwa sells home-made zobo drinks in Jos and wrote this first draft.
steps: Draft (52 words): 'We wish to inform our esteemed customers that we are now in the business of producing very high quality and really refreshing zobo drinks that are made with the best ingredients in order to satisfy your thirst. Kindly contact us for more information about prices and delivery. Thank you.'
She cuts filler ('we wish to inform', 'very', 'really', 'in order to') and vague words ('best ingredients').
She adds specifics: ingredients, size, price, delivery time.

Final (36 words): 'Chilled zobo made with hibiscus, ginger and pineapple, no artificial colour. 50cl bottles, about N700 each or N8,000 for 12. Delivered cold in Jos by 1pm. Reply ZOBO with how many you want.'
blocks.result: The edited version is shorter but says much more: what it is made of, the size, the price, the delivery time and exactly how to order.

blocks.text: A/B testing: let customers decide

An **A/B test** compares two versions of the same copy, version A and version B, that differ in only **one thing**, such as the headline or the call to action. You show both to similar audiences and measure which gets a better result. If you change many things at once, you will not know which change made the difference.

blocks.title: The A/B testing cycle
items: Pick one thing to test
Write versions A and B
Show both fairly
Measure one result
Keep the winner
blocks.caption: Each round teaches you one thing about your customers; then you test the next thing.

blocks.title: Worked example: testing two status headlines
blocks.context: For example, Hauwa wants to know whether a price-led or a taste-led first line gets more zobo orders on her WhatsApp status.
steps: Thing to test: the first line only. Picture, price, CTA and posting time stay the same.
Version A: 'Chilled zobo, 12 bottles for about N8,000.'
Version B: 'Hibiscus, ginger and pineapple, served ice cold.'
She posts A on Monday and Wednesday, and B on Tuesday and Thursday, at 10am each day, for two weeks.
She records views and ZOBO replies in a simple sheet: A got 410 views and 21 replies in total; B got 395 views and 9 replies.
Reply rate: A is 21 out of 410, about 5.1%; B is 9 out of 395, about 2.3%.
blocks.result: The price-led headline got more than twice the reply rate in her test, so she keeps it and next tests the call to action. She remembers that one small test is a clue, not a law, and re-tests later.

blocks.title: Tools that test for you
blocks.text: Meta Ads Manager has a built-in A/B test feature that splits your audience and compares versions of an ad. Most email tools, such as Mailchimp and Brevo, can split-test subject lines. For WhatsApp status and posts, a simple notebook or Google Sheets record like the table above works well.

items: **Good things to test first:** the headline or first line, how the price is shown, the call to action wording, the picture, and the offer (for example free delivery versus a small discount).
**Measure what matters:** replies, clicks, orders or payments, not only likes.
**Write down a guess before you start,** for example 'I think the price-led line will get more replies', so you learn from being wrong too.

blocks.text: Be fair: run both versions at similar times, to similar audiences, for long enough to see a pattern. Small numbers can mislead, so if the results are close, treat it as a tie and test something with a bigger difference.

takeaways: Edit with a checklist: reader, first line, benefits, specifics, proof, action, truth
Cut filler, use short words and read your copy aloud
An A/B test changes only one thing and measures one result
Record results in a sheet and treat small tests as clues to re-check

activity.title: Edit one piece and run one A/B test
steps: Take one of your recent posts and edit it with the seven-point checklist.
Count the words before and after.
Choose one element to test (headline, price display or CTA) and write versions A and B.
Post them fairly over at least one week and record views and replies in a sheet.
Calculate each reply rate and decide what you will keep or test next.
activity.evidence: Your before-and-after edit, word counts and your A/B test record sheet with reply rates

quiz.q: In Before, After, Bridge, what is the 'bridge'?
options: How the product took the customer from the before to the after
The customer's original problem
The price of the product
A testimonial from another customer
quiz.explain: The bridge explains what made the change possible: your product or service, and how the reader can get the same result.

quiz.q: A customer sent Sade a lovely WhatsApp message about her sandals. What should Sade do before posting a screenshot?
options: Post it immediately; it is her chat
Add a few extra compliments to make it stronger
Ask permission and hide the customer's number and photo
Change the customer's name to a celebrity
quiz.explain: Ethical testimonials need permission, keep the customer's meaning and protect private details.

quiz.q: Bukola's catering page title is 'Home'. Which new title is best for search?
options: Welcome!!!
Small Chops Delivery in Ibadan | Bukky's Kitchen
Best best best small chops Ibadan cheap
Page 1
quiz.explain: A clear title with the main phrase customers search and the brand name helps both Google and readers. Repeating keywords is keyword stuffing.

quiz.q: Hauwa tests a new headline AND a new picture AND a new price on the same day. What is the problem?
options: She posted too early
A/B tests need at least five versions
Prices cannot be tested
She changed several things, so she cannot tell which one caused the result
quiz.explain: A fair A/B test changes only one element so the result can be linked to that change.

quiz.q: Version A got 21 replies from 410 views. Version B got 9 replies from 395 views. What should Hauwa conclude?
options: A had a higher reply rate in this test, so keep A and keep testing
B is better because it had fewer views
The results prove A will always win
The test is useless because the views were not identical
quiz.explain: A's reply rate was about 5.1% against about 2.3% for B. That is a useful clue to act on, while re-testing later because small tests can mislead.

quiz.q: A buyer says 'Your sandals are too expensive.' Which reply in your copy is strongest?
options: Argue that she does not understand quality
Cut the price in half immediately
Explain what makes them last, show cost over time if true, and offer a cheaper style
Ignore the comment
quiz.explain: Answering the price objection with value, reduced risk and an option respects the buyer and keeps the sale possible.

finalQuiz.q: Which three things should every piece of sales copy have?
options: A logo, a slogan and a hashtag
One reader, one offer and one action
Three emojis, a price and a phone number
A story, a discount and a deadline
finalQuiz.explain: Copy works when it speaks to one clear reader about one offer and asks for one action.

finalQuiz.q: Funmi says 'My son tears his school shoes before the term ends.' For a shoe seller, this sentence is best used as:
options: A pain point to open the copy with
A feature of the shoes
A call to action
A meta description
finalQuiz.explain: It is a real pain point in the customer's own words, ideal for a first line that makes the right reader stop.

finalQuiz.q: A brand voice guide says 'Warm, confident, playful.' Which line fits it best for an apology about a late delivery?
options: LOL rain did us again
Kindly be informed of the delay
I am sorry your order is late. The driver will reach you by 4:30pm, and I will share his location now.
No comment
finalQuiz.explain: The voice stays warm, but the tone for an apology should be calm, direct and specific.

finalQuiz.q: Which sentence is a benefit, not a feature?
options: 12-hour battery
Stainless steel body
1.5-litre capacity
You can sleep through the night when light goes off
finalQuiz.explain: A benefit describes what the feature does for the customer. The others are facts about the product.

finalQuiz.q: What does the 'Ultra-specific' part of the 4 U's ask you to add to a headline?
options: Details such as numbers, places, times or sizes
More exclamation marks
A long story
Your company registration number
finalQuiz.explain: Specific details make a headline believable and easy to picture, for example '48 hours' or 'in Enugu'.

finalQuiz.q: Tolu has five items to promote today on WhatsApp status. What is the best approach?
options: One flyer with all five items and 'Order now'
Five separate statuses, each with one idea, posted as a sequence
No status, only a broadcast to everyone
One text status listing all prices
finalQuiz.explain: One idea per status, in a planned sequence, is easier to read and lets each item get attention.

finalQuiz.q: A WhatsApp click-to-chat link for 0805 555 1234 with a pre-filled message should begin:
options: https://whatsapp.com/08055551234
finalQuiz.explain: Use 234 plus the number without the leading zero, spaces, dashes or plus sign, then ?text= for the pre-filled message.

finalQuiz.q: Which framework fits a generator repair ad best, and why?
options: AIDA, because repairs are about desire
Neither; ads should only list prices
BAB, because it is only used for repairs
PAS, because the reader feels a clear, urgent problem
finalQuiz.explain: PAS starts with a felt problem and its cost, which matches repair services well.

finalQuiz.q: On a sales page, where should frequently asked questions usually appear?
options: Before the headline
Near the end, after the offer, to settle remaining doubts before the final call to action
Nowhere; FAQs reduce sales
Only in a separate PDF
finalQuiz.explain: The FAQ handles objections that remain after the reader has seen the offer, just before she decides.

finalQuiz.q: Ifeoma wants to add new customers to her broadcast list. What should she do first?
options: Ask for their permission and tell them how to opt out
Add them all and see who complains
Send them ten messages to introduce herself
Buy more contacts to grow the list faster
finalQuiz.explain: Permission respects customers and Nigeria's Data Protection Act, and willing subscribers respond better.

finalQuiz.q: Which use of a testimonial is ethical?
options: Writing a review yourself under a friend's name
Showing a rare dramatic skin result as typical
Sharing a real customer's words with permission and her number hidden
Hiding that the reviewer received the product free
finalQuiz.explain: Ethical testimonials are real, shared with permission, keep the meaning, protect privacy and disclose any gifts.

finalQuiz.q: Hauwa's version A got 21 replies from 410 views and version B got 9 replies from 395 views, with only the headline changed. What is A's approximate reply rate?
finalQuiz.explain: 21 divided by 410 is about 0.051, or 5.1%. B's rate is about 2.3%, so A did better in this test.

capstone.title: Copywriting for Sales Practical Evidence Portfolio
capstone.brief: Produce a complete copy kit for one real product or service you sell (or a business you help): a customer profile, headlines, product description, status series, Instagram caption, an ad, a short sales page, a broadcast, an email, a customer story, objection answers and one A/B test with results.
steps: Choose one product or service and build its customer profile from at least 20 real chats, comments or reviews.
Write ten headlines, score them on the 4 U's and choose two to test.
Write a four-part product description, a five-status WhatsApp series and one Instagram caption with alt text.
Write one Meta ad using PAS and one using AIDA, checking every line against Meta's personal attributes rule.
Draft a one-page sales page with headline, benefits, proof, offer, FAQ and call to action, plus a working wa.me or payment link.
Write one permission-based WhatsApp broadcast and a three-email sequence outline.
Write one Before-After-Bridge customer story with written permission, and answers to your five most common objections.
Edit everything with the seven-point checklist, run one fair A/B test for at least a week and record the results.
evidence: Customer profile table and the list of real customer words it came from
Scored headline list and final product description
Screenshots of the status series and Instagram caption as posted
Both ad drafts and the sales page draft or live link
Broadcast, email outline, customer story with permission message, and objection answers
A/B test record sheet with reply rates and your decision
